vignette:
The Weight of Gravity

Marcus is a 56-year-old combat pilot with over three decades of military aviation behind him - a career built on precision, composure, and the ability to make split-second decisions at thirty thousand feet. He has flown through hostile airspace, navigated mechanical failures mid-mission, and brought damaged aircraft home more times than he cares to count. Danger, in his world, has always been something he managed. Something he controlled. Until the day it managed him.

Four years ago, during a routine training exercise, Marcus experienced a catastrophic hydraulic failure that left him with almost no control of his aircraft. For eleven minutes - a duration he can recite to the second - he fought to keep the jet from entering a terminal spin. He ejected at the last possible moment, sustaining a fractured vertebra, a shattered right wrist, and a severe concussion when he struck the ground. He watched the aircraft explode from the hillside where he landed. He has not spoken about those eleven minutes to anyone, including his wife of twenty-eight years, Elena.

In the weeks after the accident, Marcus threw himself into rehabilitation with the same discipline that had defined his career. He told himself - and anyone who asked - that he had been through worse. He returned to limited flight duties within six months, which felt, at the time, like proof that he was fine. But something had quietly broken loose inside him, and it has been drifting ever since.

He now sleeps in fragments. Most nights, he wakes between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, sheets soaked, certain he is still in the cockpit and that the ground is rising toward him. He lies rigid in the dark, listening to Elena breathe, unwilling to wake her and unable to explain what is happening even if he did. During the day, he moves through the world with a hypervigilance that exhausts him - scanning rooms when he enters them, sitting with his back to walls, flinching at sounds that no one else seems to notice. A car backfiring in the base parking lot last spring sent him flat against a concrete wall, hands shaking, before he could register what he was doing.

In the cockpit, the man who once flew by instinct now second-guesses every instrument reading. He runs checklists he has memorized for thirty years as though seeing them for the first time, terrified that he has missed something, that something is about to fail. His commanding officer has noticed the hesitation. Marcus knows he has noticed. This knowledge sits in his chest like a stone.

At home, he has become someone Elena describes, quietly and carefully, as "far away." He sits at the dinner table and cannot follow the conversation. He cancels plans with friends, citing fatigue he cannot fully explain. He has stopped flying the small civilian Cessna he kept at a regional airfield for pleasure - a ritual he once described as the only place he felt completely himself. He drove to the airfield twice in the past year and both times sat in the car for an hour before turning around and going home.

Marcus does not think of himself as someone who suffers. That is not the vocabulary his life has given him. What he thinks, in the quieter moments, is that he used to understand the sky - its physics, its risks, its rules - and that understanding was the foundation of everything he knew about himself. Now, when he looks up, something in him braces. The sky looks the same as it always did. He is the thing that has changed, and he cannot find the instrument panel that tells him how far off course he has drifted, or whether there is still enough altitude to recover.
